history.q: According to tradition, in which year was Rome founded?
history.fact: Legend says Romulus founded Rome on 21 April 753 BCE, and the city still celebrates that date as its birthday, the Natale di Roma.

history.q: Which general led the 1860 'Expedition of the Thousand' that helped unify Italy?
history.fact: Garibaldi's volunteers, nicknamed the 'Redshirts', sailed from near Genoa in 1860 and went on to conquer Sicily and Naples.

history.q: In which year did the eruption of Mount Vesuvius bury Pompeii?
history.fact: Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters; his uncle, Pliny the Elder, died while leading a rescue mission across the bay.

history.q: Which banking family dominated Renaissance Florence and patronised artists like Michelangelo?
history.fact: The Medici produced popes Leo X and Clement VII and two queens of France, Catherine and Marie de' Medici.

history.q: Who became Rome's first emperor in 27 BCE?
history.fact: The month of August is named after Augustus; Julius Caesar, his great-uncle, was dictator but never emperor.

history.q: Who became the first King of a unified Italy in 1861?
history.fact: Rome's enormous white Vittoriano monument, jokingly nicknamed 'the wedding cake' or 'the typewriter', was built in his honour.

history.q: Which Germanic leader deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman emperor, in 476 CE?
history.fact: The deposed teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus was not killed but pensioned off to live in a villa near Naples.

history.q: In which year did Mussolini's Fascists stage the 'March on Rome'?
history.fact: King Victor Emmanuel III invited Mussolini to form a government; Mussolini himself arrived in Rome by overnight train from Milan.

history.q: Which city was the capital of the Kingdom of Italy from 1865 to 1871, before Rome?
history.fact: Italy's capital moved from Turin to Florence in 1865, then to Rome in 1871 after the city was taken from the Papal States.

history.q: In which year did mutinous troops of Emperor Charles V carry out the infamous Sack of Rome?
history.fact: During the sack, Pope Clement VII fled along a fortified passage to Castel Sant'Angelo while the Swiss Guard fought a heroic rearguard.

technology.q: Guglielmo Marconi is best known for pioneering which technology?
technology.fact: Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics, and in 1901 sent a radio signal across the Atlantic from Cornwall to Newfoundland.

technology.q: Alessandro Volta's 'voltaic pile' of 1800 was the first what?
technology.fact: The unit of electric potential, the volt, is named in Volta's honour; Napoleon later made him a count.

technology.q: In 1610, which scientist discovered four large moons of Jupiter with his telescope?
technology.fact: Galileo named the moons the 'Medicean Stars' to flatter his patrons; today Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto are called the Galilean moons.

technology.q: Which Renaissance genius filled notebooks with designs for flying machines, written in mirror script?
technology.fact: One of Leonardo's notebooks, the Codex Leicester, was bought by Bill Gates in 1994 for about 30 million dollars.

technology.q: Which Italian physicist led the team that achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in 1942?
technology.fact: Chicago Pile-1 was built under the stands of a university sports field; the element fermium is named after Fermi.

technology.q: Which Paduan instrument maker invented the piano around 1700 in Florence?
technology.fact: Cristofori's instrument could play soft and loud, hence 'pianoforte'; his 1720 piano at New York's Met is the oldest surviving one.

technology.q: Evangelista Torricelli invented which instrument in 1643?
technology.fact: Torricelli had been Galileo's assistant; a unit of pressure, the torr, is named after him.

technology.q: In which city was the carmaker FIAT founded in 1899?
technology.fact: FIAT stands for Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino; its old Lingotto factory famously had a test track on its roof.

technology.q: Which Italian chemist shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on polymers such as polypropylene?
technology.fact: Natta's team in Milan made isotactic polypropylene in 1954, a tough plastic now found in everything from car bumpers to food tubs.

technology.q: Rita Levi-Montalcini won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Medicine for discovering what?
technology.fact: Barred from university by Fascist racial laws, she ran experiments on chick embryos in a lab in her bedroom; she lived to 103.

art.q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
art.fact: Michelangelo painted the ceiling between 1508 and 1512, though he always considered himself first and foremost a sculptor.

art.q: Who painted 'The Last Supper' on a refectory wall in Milan?
art.fact: Leonardo experimented with paint on dry plaster, so it began flaking in his lifetime; sandbags helped it survive a 1943 bombing raid.
Dante simply called it 'Commedia'; the word 'Divina' was added later, popularised by Boccaccio's praise of the poem.

art.q: Which composer wrote the operas 'Aida' and 'La Traviata'?
art.fact: Aida had its world premiere in Cairo in 1871, at the Khedivial Opera House.
The Birth of Venus hangs in Florence's Uffizi Gallery, close to Botticelli's other great mythological painting, Primavera.

art.q: The aria 'Nessun dorma' comes from which Puccini opera?
art.fact: Puccini died before finishing Turandot; at the 1926 premiere, conductor Toscanini stopped the performance where Puccini's music ended.

art.q: Which Venetian composer wrote 'The Four Seasons'?
art.fact: Vivaldi, an ordained priest nicknamed 'the Red Priest' for his red hair, taught music at a Venetian orphanage for girls.

art.q: Which director made the 1960 film 'La Dolce Vita'?
art.fact: The film's celebrity photographer, Paparazzo, gave the world the word 'paparazzi'.

art.q: Which architect designed the great dome of Florence Cathedral?
art.fact: Built between 1420 and 1436 without a wooden support frame, it remains the largest brick dome ever constructed.

art.q: Which Baroque painter, famed for dramatic light and shadow, painted 'The Calling of Saint Matthew' in Rome?
art.fact: Caravaggio's life was as dramatic as his art: he fled Rome in 1606 after killing a man in a brawl.

politics.q: How many consuls jointly led the Roman Republic each year?
politics.fact: Consuls served one-year terms, and Romans identified each year by naming the two consuls in office.

politics.q: What title did Benito Mussolini adopt as leader of Fascist Italy?
politics.fact: Mussolini was voted down by his own Fascist Grand Council in July 1943 and then arrested on the king's orders.

politics.q: The 1957 treaty that created the European Economic Community was signed in which city?
politics.fact: Six countries signed the Treaty of Rome on 25 March 1957, in a palace on the city's Capitoline Hill.

politics.q: Which Florentine diplomat wrote 'The Prince', a classic of political theory?
politics.fact: Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513 after being forced out of office in Florence; it was only published in 1532, after his death.

politics.q: In which year did Italians vote in a referendum to replace the monarchy with a republic?
politics.fact: King Umberto II reigned for only about a month, earning the nickname 'the May King', before leaving for exile in Portugal.

politics.q: What is the lower house of Italy's Parliament called?
politics.fact: The Chamber of Deputies meets in Palazzo Montecitorio, while the Senate sits in nearby Palazzo Madama.

politics.q: Which Roman palace is the official residence of the President of Italy?
politics.fact: The Quirinal was built as a summer residence for popes, then housed Italy's kings before becoming the presidents' home.

politics.q: Which 1929 agreement established Vatican City as an independent state?
politics.fact: Covering about 44 hectares, Vatican City is the smallest independent state in the world.

politics.q: On what date did the Constitution of the Italian Republic come into force?
politics.fact: One of the constitution's final provisions explicitly forbids re-forming the dissolved Fascist party in any form.

politics.q: Which former Prime Minister was kidnapped and killed by the Red Brigades in 1978?
politics.fact: Moro, five times Prime Minister, was seized in Rome in March 1978; his body was found in a car on Via Caetani that May.

current-affairs.q: Who became Italy's first female Prime Minister in October 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Meloni leads Brothers of Italy, a party she co-founded in 2012 that topped the September 2022 general election.

current-affairs.q: Which team did Italy beat in the final of UEFA Euro 2020, played in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Italy won on penalties at Wembley; goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma was named player of the tournament.

current-affairs.q: Which former European Central Bank president became Italy's Prime Minister in February 2021?
current-affairs.fact: As ECB president in 2012, Draghi calmed markets by pledging to do 'whatever it takes' to preserve the euro.

current-affairs.q: Which Italian tennis player won the 2024 Australian Open men's singles title?
current-affairs.fact: Raised in German-speaking South Tyrol, Sinner was a champion junior skier; in June 2024 he became the first Italian to top the ATP singles rankings.

current-affairs.q: Which Italian rock band won the Eurovision Song Contest in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Måneskin, formed in Rome, won with 'Zitti e buoni'; the band's name means 'moonlight' in Danish.

current-affairs.q: Who was re-elected as President of Italy in January 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Mattarella became only the second Italian president to win a second term, after Giorgio Napolitano in 2013.

current-affairs.q: Which northern region was the epicentre of Italy's first COVID-19 wave in early 2020?
current-affairs.fact: The Lombard town of Codogno recorded Italy's first known locally transmitted COVID-19 case in February 2020.

current-affairs.q: Which architect designed Genoa's San Giorgio Bridge, opened in 2020 to replace the collapsed Morandi Bridge?
current-affairs.fact: Renzo Piano was born in Genoa and donated his design for the new bridge to his home city.

current-affairs.q: Italy hosted the June 2024 G7 leaders' summit in which southern region?
current-affairs.fact: The summit at Borgo Egnazia included Pope Francis, the first pope to take part in a G7 summit, who spoke about artificial intelligence.

current-affairs.q: In 2023, Italy won tennis's Davis Cup for the first time since which year?
current-affairs.fact: Italy beat Australia in the 2023 final in Málaga, with Jannik Sinner winning his key matches.

general.q: Which Italian city is built on more than 100 small islands in a lagoon?
general.fact: Venice spreads across 118 small islands linked by more than 400 bridges.

general.q: Which city is the traditional home of pizza?
general.fact: In 2017, UNESCO added the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

general.q: In which city does the famous Leaning Tower stand?
general.fact: The bell tower began leaning within a few years of building work starting in 1173, due to soft ground; it took about two centuries to finish.

general.q: Which active volcano towers over eastern Sicily?
general.fact: Etna is one of the world's most active volcanoes and was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013.

general.q: What is the longest river in Italy?
general.fact: The Po flows about 650 km from Monte Viso in the Alps to the Adriatic Sea, crossing Italy's most productive farmland.

general.q: Besides Vatican City, which independent country is completely surrounded by Italy?
general.fact: San Marino claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic, with a traditional founding date of 301 CE.

general.q: What is the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea?
general.fact: Sicily has been ruled by Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Normans and Spaniards, all of whom left traces in its food and architecture.

general.q: How many times has Italy's men's team won the FIFA World Cup?
general.fact: Italy won in 1934, 1938, 1982 and 2006; the 2006 final against France in Berlin was decided on penalties.

general.q: Which Italian region is home to Parmigiano Reggiano and traditional balsamic vinegar of Modena?
general.fact: Emilia-Romagna is also motor country: Ferrari, Lamborghini and Ducati are all based there.

general.q: The five Cinque Terre villages lie on the coast of which region?
general.fact: Of the five villages, only Corniglia does not sit directly on the sea; it perches on a clifftop instead.
